title: SLI, SLO, SLA and error budgets
objectives: Distinguish an SLI, an SLO and an SLA and say who each is for
Derive an error budget from an SLO and use it to prioritise work
Choose user-centric SLIs instead of infrastructure metrics
Set an external SLA with a safety margin over the internal SLO

sources.title: SLA, SLO and SLI compared
sources.reviewDepth: Page content retrieved as an automated summary; re-read the page itself before relying on any figure.

verificationNotes: The page recommends the Google SRE Book chapter on service level objectives. It was not consulted for this lesson; read it as supplementary material before the Defend step.
The page has no dedicated pitfalls section. The cautions listed here are the ones the page raises in passing.

sections.heading: Three terms, three jobs
sections.body:
SLI (Service Level Indicator): a quantitative measure of how a service is performing. It is the raw data.
SLO (Service Level Objective): a target value or range for an SLI. An internal reliability benchmark that keeps quality high before contractual obligations are at risk.
SLA (Service Level Agreement): a formal contract with the customer stating the promised service level. It usually includes SLOs and spells out consequences for failure, such as refunds, service credits or termination.

In short: SLIs measure, SLOs set the internal target, SLAs make promises with penalties.

sections.heading: Examples the page gives
sections.body:
SLIs: availability (share of successful HTTP requests, with a note that whether 4xx responses count depends on whether user errors are excluded); latency (share of API requests under a threshold, such as p95 under 150ms); throughput (transactions per second); freshness (share of records loaded within 10 minutes); quality (share of searches returning complete results rather than a degraded fallback).
SLOs: 99.9% availability over a rolling 30 days; 95% of API calls under 200ms per month; at least 1,000 transactions per second in core trading hours.
SLAs: 99.9% monthly uptime, with a 10% invoice credit below 99.9% and a 30% credit below 99.0%; P1 incidents acknowledged within 15 minutes with updates every 30 minutes; 11 nines annual data durability with compensation for permanent loss.

sections.heading: Error budgets
sections.body: An error budget follows from an SLO. A 99.9% target leaves a 0.1% budget for unreliability. Teams can spend that budget on releases, updates and calculated risks. When it runs out, the focus moves to stability.

sections.heading: Guidance for CTOs
sections.body:
Prioritisation: a healthy budget supports shipping fast; an exhausted one shifts work to reliability, technical debt and performance.
Realistic targets: align SLOs with product management so nobody demands 100% availability, which the page calls unachievable and expensive.
Safety margin: external SLAs should be more lenient than internal SLOs. The page's example pairs an internal 99.9% SLO with an external 99.0% or 99.5% SLA, giving on-call engineers time to respond before there is financial or legal exposure.
User-centric indicators: SLIs should reflect user experience. The page says 95% CPU utilisation is a weak indicator if users still get fast, correct responses, and warns that poor indicators cause alert fatigue.

workedExample.title: What 99.9% means in minutes (arithmetic, not from the page)
workedExample.body: A 30-day month has 30 x 24 x 60 = 43,200 minutes. A 99.9% SLO allows 0.1% of that, which is 43.2 minutes of unreliability. A 99.99% SLO allows 4.32 minutes. Each extra nine cuts the budget by a factor of ten, which is why the page warns that chasing 100% is unachievable and expensive: the CTO question is what each nine costs to engineer and whether customers will pay for it.

misconceptions: Treating SLO and SLA as the same thing. One is an internal goal, the other a contract with penalties.
Setting the external SLA as strict as the internal SLO, which leaves no buffer.
Choosing indicators that are easy to measure (CPU) rather than ones users feel (latency, errors).
Thinking a 100% target is a sign of ambition. The page calls it unachievable and expensive.
learn.explainTask: In 150 words or fewer, tell a product manager why the team should not promise customers the same number it targets internally, and what the error budget lets the team do.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which of the three is a formal contract with the customer, typically with consequences such as service credits?
knowledgeCheck.why: The SLA is the contractual agreement with penalties for failure.

knowledgeCheck.question: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO. What is its error budget?
knowledgeCheck.why: The page states that a 99.9% target leaves a 0.1% budget for unreliability.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does the page say the external SLA should be more lenient than the internal SLO?
options: To make the product look cheaper
To give on-call engineers time to respond before financial or legal exposure
Because customers do not care about reliability
knowledgeCheck.why: The safety margin buys response time before penalties apply.

knowledgeCheck.question: According to the page, which is the better indicator of service health for users?
options: The share of API requests answered under a latency threshold
knowledgeCheck.why: The page prefers user-centric indicators and says CPU alone is weak if users still get fast, correct responses.

knowledgeCheck.question: The error budget is exhausted. What does the page say the team should prioritise?
knowledgeCheck.why: An exhausted budget shifts priority to stability work.

build.business: Cretek needs reliability targets that are honest, measurable and tied to decisions about when to ship and when to stop and fix.
build.problem: Define SLIs, SLOs, an error budget policy and a proposed external SLA for one real Cretek service, with measurement.
requirements: Choose one Cretek service and say who its users are
At least three SLIs that reflect user experience, each with an exact measurement definition (what counts as good and valid)
An SLO for each, with a window, and a computed error budget in minutes or requests
A proposed external SLA that is more lenient than the SLOs, with the margin justified
An error budget policy: what the team does when the budget is healthy and when it is exhausted
A script or query that computes SLI values from real or labelled simulated data
constraints: No invented Cretek reliability figures. Use real data or label the data simulated
build.design: Document where each SLI is measured (client, load balancer, application) and the failure modes that measurement point cannot see.
tasks: Write the SLI definitions and SLOs
Compute error budgets and document the arithmetic
Implement the SLI calculation with tests
Write the error budget policy and external SLA proposal
Document operational considerations: alerting, who is paged, review cadence
acceptance: Every SLI is user-centric and measurable from data you can show
Budgets are computed correctly and checked by tests
External SLA is more lenient than internal SLOs with a written reason
Policy states a concrete action when the budget is exhausted
Data is labelled REAL or SIMULATED
build.deliverable: A document plus script/tests in a repository, linked or referenced.

defend.scenario: A prospective enterprise customer is reading your proposed SLA and wants a stronger one.
prompts: Why should I accept 99.5% when your own target is 99.9%?
Show me how you measure availability. What failures would your measurement miss?
What happens to me if you miss it? Why that remedy?
Your budget is gone halfway through the month. Walk me through what changes at Cretek.
What would it cost you to give me 99.99%, and would you?

rubric.criterion: Correct distinction and use of SLI, SLO, SLA and budget
Commercial reasoning about cost of each nine and the margin
Concrete operating response when the budget is exhausted
